opinions.rationale: Inverted prior favors solutions that license transfer of successful A-in-D replications to B-in-D or A-in-E. BenchExCal (Wang et al. 2025) is exactly that transfer procedure for indication expansion: benchmark an existing-indication trial in the database, then calibrate a subsequent database study for the expanded question using the observed RCT–database differences. Kirchgesner et al. (2024) state a related trial-calibration approach for questions RCTs never answered. Heyard et al. (2024) and the BMJ 2026 concordance meta-analysis already move from a global agreement rate toward design-conditional agreement (protocol match, baseline balance, outcome quality, claims vs other sources). Prospective prediction projects (GRADE, semaglutide phase IV, FDA prediction workstream) partially remove design-calibration by freezing protocols before trial readout. None of this is a completed, general statistical theory that quantifies how much confidence transfers to arbitrary new questions or databases, and BenchExCal’s empirical evaluation is still planned (simulation plus five examples), not finished. The six-cause attribution problem for single discrepancies remains open. Saying there is “no theory” is therefore too strong; the gap is the lack of a validated general theory and completed prospective hierarchical calibration, not a blank slate.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: There is no validated, general theory that licenses quantitative transfer of confidence from successful replications of selected favorable trials to arbitrary new questions or databases; proposed frameworks (BenchExCal, trial calibration) and design-conditional concordance analyses exist but are incomplete or unevaluated for that licensing role.

resolving_work.title: A Benchmark, Expand, and Calibration (BenchExCal) Trial Emulation Approach for Using Real-World Evidence to Support Indication Expansions: Design and Process for a Planned Empirical Evaluation
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Proposes an operational theory for transferring a successful existing-indication emulation (question A in database D) into a calibrated second-stage emulation for an expanded indication (question B in D), with simulation and five planned empirical evaluations. Directly addresses the report’s missing transfer step, though as proposal plus planned evaluation rather than finished validation.
resolving_work.quote: Confidence in the validity of findings from cohort studies conducted using databases (hereafter "database study") to support indication expansions could be increased through a structured benchmarking process of an initial database study against RCT evidence followed by calibration of a subsequent database study based on differences in results observed in the initial RCT-database pair. This paper proposes a benchmark, expand, and calibration (BenchExCal) approach to trial emulation and describes the design and process for evaluating the performance of the approach through both simulation studies; five planned empirical examples are also described.

resolving_work.title: Strengthening Real-World Evidence on Question Not Answered by Randomized Trials: A Trial Calibration Approach
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Articulates trial calibration as the route from benchmarked emulation of an answered question to RWE on a related unanswered question, the same transfer structure the problem says is missing.

resolving_work.title: Design differences and variation in results between randomised trials and non-randomised emulations: meta-analysis of RCT-DUPLICATE data
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Models concordance variation as a function of design and population emulation differences rather than a single global rate, which is the hierarchical/conditional direction the report proposes.

resolving_work.title: Concordance between target trial emulation and randomised controlled trials: systematic review and meta-analysis
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Estimates design-conditional concordance (closer emulation; baseline imbalance; hospital-initiated treatment; outcome emulation quality; claims data) across 107 pairs, so agreement is already treated as a conditional quantity, not only a global rate. Does not solve transfer to unselected questions.
resolving_work.quote: Among 107 target trial emulation-randomised controlled trial pairs, the Pearson correlation coefficient was 0.59 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.45 to 0.70), standardised difference agreement was 79% (85/107), and summary ratio of ratios was 0.96 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.01; I2=36%). In 63 pairs with closer emulation of trial design, a higher level of agreement was observed, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.83 (0.73 to 0.89) and standardised difference agreement of 87% (55/63).

opinions.rationale: The claim that benchmarking “nonetheless reports success or failure as a binary label” is not faithful to the field’s primary programs or to the report’s own cited works. RCT-DUPLICATE and Franklin-line methods report regulatory/significance agreement, estimate agreement, and standardized-difference agreement together; the BMJ 2026 meta-analysis leads with Pearson correlation, ICC, ratio of ratios, standardized-difference agreement, and Bland–Altman, and only secondarily with binary metrics. Köppe, Micheloud, Erdmann, Heyard, and Held (2025) go further: they replace the two-trials (regulatory agreement) rule with the graded sceptical p-value, which uses both p-values, effect sizes, and relative precision, and invert it to combined confidence intervals; they apply it to 29 RCT-DUPLICATE pairs. ISPOR Europe 2024 also floated enhanced multi-metric RCT–RWE agreement assessments for HTA. What remains open is universal adoption, explicit estimand alignment (how much estimand difference is tolerable), and routine prediction-interval coverage that treats trial sampling error as a distribution. Binary labels are still convenient for secondary citation and still appear beside continuous metrics, but they are not the sole or best existing practice. The report’s proposed direction (ratio of effects, absolute difference, standardized agreement, prediction-interval coverage, prospective forecasts) is largely what the better literature already does or is building.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Binary agreement labels remain common in secondary reporting of benchmarking and are still listed among primary metrics, even though leading programs and the 2026 concordance meta-analysis already report continuous multi-metric comparisons; a fully estimand-calibrated prediction-interval criterion that cleanly separates estimand mismatch from random error is not yet standard.

resolving_work.title: Emulation of Randomized Clinical Trials With Nonrandomized Database Analyses: Results of 32 Clinical Trials
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Already reports multiple agreement metrics (not a single pass/fail label) across 32 prespecified emulations; this is the report’s own cited “most careful existing treatment of the labeling question.”

resolving_work.title: Concordance between target trial emulation and randomised controlled trials: systematic review and meta-analysis
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Primary reporting is continuous and multi-metric (correlation 0.59/0.83, ratio of ratios, standardized-difference rates, design-feature regressions), not a binary success label. Directly undercuts the claim that benchmarking only reports binary agreement.
resolving_work.quote: Most target trial emulation-randomised controlled trial pairs met one or more of the binary agreement metrics for concordance (table 3): standardised difference agreement (85/107; 79%), estimate agreement (82/107; 77%), full agreement for statistical significance (53/107; 50%), and partial agreement for statistical significance (20/41; 49%). The Pearson coefficient between target trial emulation-randomised controlled trial pairs was 0.59 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.45 to 0.70), and the intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.56 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.68), consistent with moderate correlation.

resolving_work.title: Assessing the replicability of RCTs in RWE emulations
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Supplies a graded, calibrated alternative to binary two-trials/regulatory agreement (the sceptical p-value), depending on both p-values, effect sizes, and relative precision; extends to non-inferiority and inverted CIs; applied to RCT-DUPLICATE. Partially delivers the report’s call for calibrated comparison rather than a binary label.
resolving_work.quote: The pure assessment of the significance of the original trial and the replication study (two-trials rule – TTR) has the disadvantage that it does not directly take into account the effect sizes of the two studies. [...] The sceptical p-value can be interpreted quantitatively: Smaller pS values indicate a higher degree of replication success. [...] Conclusion: The sceptical p-value represents a valid statistical measure to assess the replicability of study results and is especially useful in the context of real-world evidence emulations.

resolving_work.title: Assessing the replicability of RCTs in RWE emulations
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Peer-reviewed publication of the sceptical p-value application to RWE emulations (same work as arXiv 2412.09334), confirming the graded metric is in the methods literature, not only a preprint.

counter_evidence.quote: Previously published literature applied the three statistical metrics used in this study to evaluate the success of the emulation. However, these metrics alone are not sufficient to determine if an emulation has been successful, as each has their limitations. Both estimate agreement and standardized difference agreement fail to incorporate the uncertainty that comes with the target trial estimate. [...] Moreover, statistical significance agreement is disproportionately harsh when estimates (or their CI limits) lay close to the null.
